subtopics.name: Care of clients with sensory impairment

questions.stem: A 22-year-old is admitted after a diving accident with a complete spinal cord injury at C4. The client is awake and anxious, with an SpO2 of 94% and a weak cough. Which nursing assessment is the priority?

options.text: Breathing effort, cough strength and vital capacity
Skin over the sacrum and heels for early pressure injury
Bowel sounds and the need for a bowel program
Readiness to learn about using a power wheelchair

rationale.correct: "C3, 4, 5 keeps the diaphragm alive": high cervical injuries threaten breathing first.

perOption.a: C3 to C5 supply the phrenic nerve to the diaphragm, so a C4 injury can cause respiratory failure.
perOption.b: This matters but comes after breathing.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Prioritize breathing in a cervical spinal cord injury.

questions.stem: A client with a T4 spinal cord injury suddenly has a pounding headache, a blood pressure of 210/110 mm Hg, flushing and sweating above the injury, and a heart rate of 50/min. The client is lying in bed. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Sit the client upright with the legs lowered
Give the PRN nifedipine for the high blood pressure
Lay the client flat to reduce the headache
Check the client's temperature and pulse oximetry

rationale.correct: Autonomic dysreflexia (injury at T6 or above): sit up, loosen clothing, find and remove the trigger (usually a full bladder, then bowel or skin), then give medication if needed.

perOption.a: Raising the head lowers the blood pressure quickly while the cause is found.
perOption.b: Medication comes after positioning and removing the trigger, if the pressure stays high.
perOption.c: Lying flat raises the blood pressure further.
perOption.d: These do not treat the emergency.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Respond to autonomic dysreflexia.

questions.stem: The nurse has sat a client with autonomic dysreflexia upright and loosened the abdominal binder. The blood pressure is still 196/104 mm Hg. The client has an indwelling catheter. What should the nurse check next?

options.text: The catheter tubing for kinks and the bladder for distention
The client's pupils, for size and how briskly they react to light
The client's capillary blood glucose level
Breath sounds in both lungs for crackles

rationale.correct: Common triggers of autonomic dysreflexia: bladder distention, fecal impaction, tight clothing and pressure injuries.

perOption.a: A full bladder from a blocked catheter is the most common trigger.
perOption.b: These are not the main cause.
perOption.c: This is not a usual trigger.
perOption.d: This is not the main cause.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify triggers of autonomic dysreflexia.

questions.stem: A client admitted 2 hours ago with an acute C6 spinal cord injury has a blood pressure of 78/40 mm Hg and a heart rate of 48/min, with warm, dry, pink skin below the injury. The hemoglobin is unchanged from admission. Which condition does the nurse suspect?

options.text: Neurogenic shock
Hypovolemic shock from internal bleeding
Autonomic dysreflexia
Early septic shock

rationale.correct: Neurogenic shock: hypotension, bradycardia and warm skin from loss of sympathetic tone after a cervical or high thoracic injury.

perOption.a: Loss of sympathetic tone causes hypotension, bradycardia and warm, dry skin.
perOption.b: Hypovolemia causes tachycardia and cool skin, and the hemoglobin is stable.
perOption.d: There are no signs of infection this early.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize neurogenic shock.

questions.stem: A client with a cervical spine fracture is going home in a halo vest. The family will help with care. Which item must be kept with the client at all times?

options.text: The wrench that removes the vest's front panel
A soft cervical collar to wear at night
Sandbags to support the head in bed
A spare set of pins for the halo ring

rationale.correct: Keep the wrench taped to the halo vest, and never use the frame to lift or move the client.

perOption.a: In a cardiac arrest, the front panel must be removed quickly for CPR.
perOption.b: The halo already stabilizes the neck.
perOption.c: These are not needed with a halo.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Ensure halo vest emergency equipment is available.

questions.stem: A client with a T10 spinal cord injury is starting a bowel program before going home to a rehabilitation unit. Which intervention should the nurse include?

options.text: A set daily time with a suppository or digital stimulation
A low-fiber diet so that the stools are smaller and easier to pass
Limiting fluids to avoid incontinence at night
Toileting only when the client feels the urge

rationale.correct: Bowel programs use regular timing, fiber, fluids and stimulation to prevent impaction, which can also trigger autonomic dysreflexia in higher injuries.

perOption.a: A consistent schedule trains the bowel and prevents incontinence and impaction.
perOption.d: The client may not feel the urge.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Plan a bowel program after spinal cord injury.

questions.stem: A client with myasthenia gravis has had a respiratory infection for 3 days and now has increasing weakness, drooping eyelids, trouble swallowing and a weak cough. The vital capacity is falling. Which nursing assessment is the priority?

options.text: Breathing, vital capacity and ability to clear secretions
Strength of the leg muscles when pushing against resistance
Skin over the sacrum and heels for redness or breakdown
Total calorie intake over the last 24 hours of the stay

rationale.correct: In myasthenic crisis, monitor breathing closely; intubation may be needed.

perOption.a: Myasthenic crisis can cause respiratory failure and may need intubation.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Prioritize assessment in a myasthenic crisis.

questions.stem: A client with myasthenia gravis who takes pyridostigmine says, "By the end of dinner I can barely chew." When should the nurse tell the client to take the medication?

options.text: 30 to 60 minutes before meals, on schedule
At bedtime so that it works overnight
Only when the weakness becomes severe
Right after each meal, with a glass of water

rationale.correct: Cholinesterase inhibitors are taken on time; too much causes cholinergic crisis with excess secretions, cramps and weakness.

perOption.a: A peak effect at mealtime helps chewing and swallowing; late doses worsen weakness.
perOption.b: This does not support daytime function.
perOption.c: It is taken on a schedule.
perOption.d: Strength is needed during the meal.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Teach timing of pyridostigmine.

questions.stem: A client with Guillain-Barré syndrome, admitted yesterday, had weakness that started in the feet and has moved up to the hips. The client now reports tingling in the hands. Which nursing action is the priority?

options.text: Monitor respiratory function, including vital capacity
Start range-of-motion exercises to prevent contractures
Give the prescribed gabapentin for the tingling
Teach the family about the expected course of recovery

rationale.correct: Guillain-Barré syndrome causes ascending paralysis; watch vital capacity and the ability to swallow.

perOption.a: Ascending paralysis can reach the respiratory muscles.
perOption.c: Discomfort matters, but breathing comes first.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Prioritize breathing in Guillain-Barré syndrome.

questions.stem: A client with multiple sclerosis says the legs feel weaker and vision blurs after a hot shower, then improves after an hour. What should the nurse teach?

options.text: "Use lukewarm water and avoid getting overheated."
"Hot showers help your muscles relax, so keep using them."
"A sauna afterward will help your circulation recover."
"These symptoms mean you're having a full relapse."

rationale.correct: Clients with MS should avoid heat, fatigue, stress and infection, which can worsen symptoms.

perOption.a: Heat slows conduction in demyelinated nerves (the Uhthoff phenomenon).
perOption.d: Brief heat-related worsening is not a true relapse.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Teach clients with MS to avoid heat.

questions.stem: A client with Parkinson disease takes carbidopa-levodopa four times a day and says the medicine "wears off" after a big steak dinner. Which instruction should the nurse give?

options.text: "Spread protein through the day rather than eating a lot at once."
"Take a vitamin B6 supplement to make the medicine work better."
"Stop the medicine right away if your urine or your sweat turns dark."
"Stand up quickly after meals to prevent dizziness."

rationale.correct: Carbidopa-levodopa: orthostatic hypotension, dyskinesias, dark urine and a protein interaction.

perOption.a: Dietary protein competes with levodopa for absorption.
perOption.b: B6 is not recommended and can reduce levodopa's effect.
perOption.c: Dark urine or sweat is harmless.
perOption.d: Orthostatic hypotension is common; the client rises slowly.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Teach about carbidopa-levodopa.

questions.stem: The nurse is assessing a 72-year-old client newly diagnosed with Parkinson disease. Which findings should the nurse expect? Select all that apply.

options.text: Tremor of the hand at rest
Slowness of movement
Muscle rigidity
Shuffling gait
Tremor only when reaching for an object
Weakness that worsens later in the day

rationale.correct: Parkinson disease: tremor at rest, rigidity, bradykinesia and postural instability (TRAP).

perOption.a: Resting tremor is a cardinal sign.
perOption.e: This intention tremor suggests a cerebellar problem.
perOption.f: This fatigable weakness suggests myasthenia gravis.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize the signs of Parkinson disease.

questions.stem: A client with Parkinson disease has fallen twice at home because the feet "stick to the floor" when starting to walk. Which instruction should the nurse give to reduce the risk of falls?

options.text: "Lift your feet and take big steps, with your feet apart."
"Walk quickly with small steps so you don't lose momentum."
"Look down at your feet while walking to watch each step."
"Keep throw rugs down so a fall is cushioned."

rationale.correct: Parkinson gait training: big steps, a wide base, swinging the arms, and rocking to start when frozen.

perOption.a: This counteracts shuffling and improves balance.
perOption.c: Looking down worsens posture and balance.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Teach fall prevention in Parkinson disease.

questions.stem: The adult daughter of a client newly diagnosed with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) asks what to expect. Which statement by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: "Thinking usually stays clear while the muscles weaken."
"The disease mainly affects feeling and sensation."
"Surgery can usually slow or stop the disease."
"Breathing muscles are not affected by ALS."

rationale.correct: ALS: progressive motor weakness with intact cognition; plan early for breathing and nutrition needs.

perOption.a: ALS affects motor neurons; most clients stay mentally alert.
perOption.d: Respiratory failure is the usual cause of death.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Understand the course of ALS.

questions.stem: A client with trigeminal neuralgia has stabbing facial pain when a breeze touches the left cheek. Which statement by the client shows correct understanding?

options.text: "I'll chew on my right side and eat lukewarm food."
"I'll rub my left cheek firmly when the pain starts."
"I'll hold an ice pack on my face during an attack."
"I'll skip meals on days when the pain is bad."

rationale.correct: Trigeminal neuralgia: avoid triggers such as touch, cold and chewing on the affected side; carbamazepine is often prescribed.

perOption.a: This avoids triggering the pain on the affected side.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Teach a client with trigeminal neuralgia.

questions.stem: A client with Bell palsy cannot close the right eye completely and says the eye feels dry. Which intervention is most important?

options.text: Artificial tears by day, eyelid taped shut at night
Ice packs held on the right side of the face each hour
Avoiding chewing on the right side for 2 weeks
Keeping the room dark at all times of day

rationale.correct: Bell palsy: protect the eye; moist heat and facial exercises help, and steroids are often prescribed.

perOption.a: This protects the cornea from drying and injury.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Protect the eye in Bell palsy.

questions.stem: A 54-year-old client in the emergency department with a migraine is prescribed sumatriptan. Which finding in the client's history should the nurse report to the provider before giving it?

options.text: Chest pain on exertion, treated with nitroglycerin
Seasonal allergies treated with loratadine
Migraines that began in the client's teens
Mild acne treated with a topical cream

rationale.correct: Triptans are contraindicated with coronary artery disease, uncontrolled hypertension and recent ergot use.

perOption.a: Triptans cause vasoconstriction and are contraindicated in coronary artery disease.
perOption.c: This is the reason for the drug.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify contraindications to triptans.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old client had cataract surgery on the left eye this morning and is going home. Which statement by the client shows a need for more teaching?

options.text: "I'll wear the eye shield when I sleep."
"I'll bend over to tie my shoes tomorrow."
"I'll call if my eye suddenly hurts a lot."
"I'll use my eye drops exactly as prescribed."

rationale.correct: After cataract surgery: avoid bending, lifting and straining, wear the shield, and report pain or vision loss.

perOption.a: The shield protects the eye.
perOption.b: Bending raises eye pressure; the client avoids bending and heavy lifting.
perOption.c: Sudden pain may signal a complication.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Teach a client after cataract surgery.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old client comes to urgent care after leaving a dark movie theater with sudden severe pain in the right eye, blurred vision, halos around lights, a headache and vomiting. The right pupil is mid-dilated and does not react. Which condition does the nurse suspect?

options.text: Acute angle-closure glaucoma
A mature cataract in the right eye
Wet macular degeneration
Bacterial conjunctivitis

rationale.correct: Acute angle-closure glaucoma needs immediate treatment to lower the eye pressure.

perOption.a: This is an emergency that can cause permanent vision loss within hours.
perOption.c: This causes central vision loss without severe pain.
perOption.d: This causes redness and discharge without vision loss or a fixed pupil.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize acute angle-closure glaucoma.

questions.stem: A client with open-angle glaucoma and asthma is starting timolol eye drops. Which instruction best reduces the risk of systemic side effects?

options.text: "Press the inner corner of the eye for 1 to 2 minutes after each drop."
"Blink rapidly several times after each drop so that it spreads out well."
"Use two drops each time to make sure enough gets in."
"Rinse your eye with water a minute after the drop."

rationale.correct: Timolol is a beta-blocker; systemic absorption can cause bradycardia and bronchospasm, which is a particular risk with asthma.

perOption.a: This blocks drainage into the tear duct and reduces systemic absorption.
perOption.b: Blinking pumps the drug into the tear duct.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Reduce systemic absorption of eye drops.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old client calls the clinic reporting sudden flashes of light, many new floaters and a shadow like a curtain coming down over the left eye. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Arrange same-day evaluation for retinal detachment
Tell the client to rest the eyes and call back in a week
Recommend lubricating drops and a cool compress
Book a routine appointment for new glasses

rationale.correct: Retinal detachment is an emergency.

perOption.a: These are classic signs; prompt surgery can save vision.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize retinal detachment.

questions.stem: A 76-year-old client has dry age-related macular degeneration in both eyes and lives alone. The client reads large-print books and wants to keep driving in daylight. Which tool should the nurse teach the client to use at home to watch for changes?

options.text: An Amsler grid
A Snellen eye chart
A home tonometer
A pinhole occluder

rationale.correct: Macular degeneration affects central vision; check daily with an Amsler grid and report new distortion.

perOption.a: The grid detects new distortion or blind spots in central vision.
perOption.b: This tests visual acuity in the clinic.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Teach home monitoring for macular degeneration.

questions.stem: The nurse is admitting an 84-year-old client with age-related hearing loss who does not have hearing aids with them. Which communication strategy is best?

options.text: Face the client and speak clearly in a lower pitch
Speak loudly directly into the client's better ear
Speak quickly so the admission takes less time
Talk while writing notes so as to save time

rationale.correct: Presbycusis affects high frequencies: face the client, speak clearly, lower the pitch and reduce background noise.

perOption.a: This helps lip-reading and uses the frequencies older adults keep.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Communicate with a client who has hearing loss.

questions.stem: A client with Ménière disease is having an acute attack of vertigo with nausea and ringing in the right ear. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Have the client lie still in a quiet, dim room
Encourage the client to walk to reset the balance
Turn on bright lights so the client can focus
Offer salty crackers to settle the nausea

rationale.correct: Ménière disease: vertigo, tinnitus and hearing loss; limit sodium and keep the client safe during attacks.

perOption.a: Movement and stimulation worsen the vertigo.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Manage an acute Ménière attack.

questions.stem: A nurse educator is reviewing four neurological disorders with new graduates on a neuro unit, using clients currently on the unit as examples. Each client was admitted with worsening symptoms of a known chronic condition. For each disorder, choose the characteristic finding the new graduates should expect to see when they assess the client.

columns.text: Ptosis that worsens later in the day

rationale.correct: Tell neurological disorders apart by their hallmark features.

perOption.r1:c2: Muscle fatigue worsens with use, so weakness increases later in the day.
perOption.r2:c1: Weakness begins in the legs and moves upward.
perOption.r4:c4: Heat slows conduction in demyelinated nerves.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Match neurological disorders to key findings.
